title: Continuous batching scheduler tuning experiments (batch size, timeout, fairness, tail latency) - run 13
content:
Summary
-------
Run 13 of our continuous-batching scheduler tuning experiments focused on exploring trade-offs between max batch size, assembly timeout, and fairness policies with an eye on tail latency (p95/p99), throughput (tokens/sec), and wasted compute. This doc captures experiment matrix, profiler findings, surprising bottlenecks, and recommended defaults for the next release.

Context / goal
----------------
- Goal: reduce p99 token latency for short requests (<= 64 tokens) while retaining high overall throughput for mixed workloads.
- Constraints: must not regress p50 by >10% or reduce aggregate tokens/sec by >8% for steady mixed workloads.
- Workload used: mix-1 (70% short chat turns ~32 tokens, 20% medium ~128 tokens, 10% long ~512 tokens).
- Test infra: 8x A100 (40GB) serving nodes; runtime commit: 0.63.2-branch-experiments (PR #482).

Experiment matrix
------------------
We ran a grid over: max_batch_size = {8, 16, 32, 64}, assemble_timeout_ms = {1, 3, 6, 12}, fairness = {fifo, size-aware, weighted-priority}. Each combination ran for 20 minutes steady-state with 5-minute ramp and 10-minute cooldown.

Key metrics collected (per-run)
- p50/p90/p95/p99 token latency (ms)
- end-to-end request latency (ms)
- tokens/sec and requests/sec
- GPU util and % time spent in small-kernel vs large-kernel paths
- queue wait time distribution
- batching efficiency (avg batch fill %, number of wasted slots)
- context-switch/syscall overhead measured with eBPF traces

Top-level results (high-level)
--------------------------------
- Best tail latency for short requests: max_batch_size=16, assemble_timeout_ms=3, fairness=size-aware. p99 token latency improved ~18% vs baseline (baseline: max_batch_size=32, timeout=6ms, fifo).
- Highest throughput: max_batch_size=64, timeout=12ms, fifo \u2014 tokens/sec +12% vs baseline, but p99 for short requests regressed by ~45% (bad for latency-sensitive features).
- Fairness: size-aware scheduling gives the best tail latency for short requests without catastrophic throughput loss (throughput down ~4% vs best-throughput config). Weighted-priority (priority to short requests) reduces short-request p99 by ~25% but increased p99 for medium+long by >30% and introduced starvation risk in synthetic skew tests.

Profiling and bottlenecks observed
----------------------------------
- Queue head-of-line blocking: Larger max_batch_size increases waiting time for short requests because they often wait for long requests to fill batch. Size-aware and weighted-priority alleviates this but at cost to fairness across longer requests.
- Assembly timeout: small timeouts (1ms) reduce p99 but increase number of small batches leading to more kernel launches and higher small-kernel overhead (~+9% GPU active time spent on kernel-launch overhead). 3ms looked like a good sweet spot.
- Lock contention: the batch-assembly lock (coarse-grained) shows increased mutex contends at high qps (seen in flamegraphs). Contention correlates with assemble_timeout < 3ms and high concurrent requester threads.
- Scheduler overhead: the per-request scheduling dequeue path uses atomic counters that are hot; adding a local per-thread buffer reduced remote atomics by ~35% and lowered CPU tail latency by ~12ms.
- KV cache & KV-copy cost: for long context requests, KV cache copy into GPU context memory dominates batch assembly time when number of kv pages > 2; this disproportionately affects medium/long requests. Consider streaming KV or lazy copy.
- Small vs large kernel mix: workloads with many small batches spend more percent time in small attention kernels which are less efficient. Observed that avg tokens/sec per GPU drops when small-batch ratio > 0.35.

Surprising findings / notes to self
-----------------------------------
- The theoretical model overestimated benefit of timeout=1ms: while p99 shrinks, overall per-token cost increases because kernel launch overhead and underfilled batches dominate.
- Weighted-priority with strict prioritization causes near-starvation in adversarial synthetic arrival patterns (10% long requests arriving in bursts push medium requests to >10s). Need aging or backpressure.
- eBPF traces showed ~20% of tail latency for short requests attributed to syscalls in user-space logging path (debug-level logs) \u2014 we should ensure logging is disabled in production builds used for benchmarks.

Detailed numbers (selected)
--------------------------
- Baseline (32,6,fifo): short-p99=182ms, short-p95=96ms, tokens/sec=1.02M, batch-fill=0.62
- Best-tail (16,3,size-aware): short-p99=150ms (-17.6%), short-p95=82ms, tokens/sec=0.98M (-3.9%), batch-fill=0.71
- High-throughput (64,12,fifo): short-p99=263ms (+44.5%), tokens/sec=1.14M (+11.8%), batch-fill=0.86
- Weighted-priority (16,3,weighted): short-p99=112ms (-38.5%), med-p99=450ms (+35%), tokens/sec=0.93M (-8.8%)

Recommended defaults for beta release
------------------------------------
- Default scheduler config: max_batch_size=16, assemble_timeout_ms=3, fairness=size-aware. Rationale: most balanced for latency-sensitive short-turn chat without too much throughput regression.
- Add a 'latency_mode' preset (latency-optimized) that sets: max_batch_size=8, assemble_timeout_ms=1, fairness=weighted-with-aging. Warn users about increased cost.
- Instrument aging in weighted-priority to prevent starvation; add an integration test (SCHED-213) that simulates adversarial bursts.

Implementation notes / follow-ups
--------------------------------
- Replace coarse batch-assembly lock with sharded assembly queues: prototype shows reduced contention and improved tail CPU latency. See PR #482 for prototype changes.
- Investigate lazy KV copy: patch branch kv-lazy-copy (bench pending) \u2014 could reduce assembly time for long requests.
- Add kernel-launch batching optimization: combine small kernel launches when multiple small batches target same model shard (requires scheduling coalescing).
- Add eBPF-based nightly profiling job to catch syscalls / logging overhead; ensure production images run with logging=error by default.

Open questions / TODOs
----------------------
- What's acceptable p99 target for short chat flows for the hosted API SLAs? (need product input).
- How does size-aware fairness interact with multi-tenant scenarios? Risk of noisy neighbors\u2014plan isolation tests.
- Evaluate impact on Dedicated nodes with reserved pools and longer-running warm caches (the dynamics may change).

Appendix: artifacts and data
---------------------------
- Raw CSVs and plotting notebooks: linked in the run artifact (artifact storage id: run-2026-02-18-sched-13) [put in Confluence run page].
- Flamegraphs (CPU/mutex): /artifacts/flamegraphs/run-13/ (attached to PR #482)
- eBPF syscall traces: /artifacts/ebpf/run-13/

Notes for review:
- Diego: please sanity-check the KV copy numbers (I may have mis-attributed some time to KV copy vs serialization).
- Arianna: pls validate the workload mix for next week's on-prem Dedicated run; we should include a tenant-isolation test.

Conclusion
----------
Size-aware scheduling with moderate batch sizes (16) and short assemble timeouts (~3ms) looks like the best default tradeoff right now. There are clear opportunities to reduce mutex contention and KV-copy overhead which could push us closer to high-throughput configs without the tail-latency regressions. Next steps: land the sharded assembly queue prototype, add aging to weighted-priority, and run Dedicated/tenant isolation experiments.

-- Marcus
